opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important question, and honestly I don't think it's guaranteed. It's something we have to design for. Open-endedness by definition means the system keeps generating novel things, and novelty on its own can drift into regions that are interesting to the algorithm but completely irrelevant to us. So the question is how you anchor it.

There are a few anchors I find convincing. The first is that the substrate these agents work on is fundamentally human. If you build an AI Scientist on top of large language models, those models have been trained on an enormous corpus of human scientific writing, debates and priorities. So their notion of what counts as interesting is, to a large degree, inherited from us. When people in the open-endedness community talk about "models of human notions of interestingness," that's essentially what an LLM gives you. It's a kind of prior over what a researcher would find surprising or worthwhile.

The second anchor is the evaluation loop. In practice, these systems are not running in a vacuum. They produce papers, code, experimental results, and those artifacts get reviewed, either by automated reviewers that are themselves calibrated on human judgments, or eventually by actual humans in the community. If the outputs aren't legible or useful to people, they don't get picked up, they don't get built upon, and that selection pressure feeds back into what the system pursues.

The third is that I don't really see the near-term picture as fully autonomous. I think it's much more of a collaboration, where humans set the high-level directions, the grand challenges if you like, and the agent does a lot of the exploration within that space. The human acts a bit like a principal investigator steering a very fast, very tireless lab. That keeps the work tethered.

That said, I want to be careful not to be naive about it. There's a real risk of the system optimizing for things that look like progress, like benchmark numbers or reviewer scores, without actually being meaningful. That's Goodhart's law applied to science. So a lot of the research challenge is building better verification, better grounding in real experiments, and keeping humans in the loop at the points where judgment really matters. If we get that right, I'm optimistic the open-endedness becomes a feature: it lets the agent find stepping stones we wouldn't have thought of, while still heading somewhere we care about.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the obvious worry with open-endedness is drift. You set a system loose to explore and it ends up optimizing for things that are interesting to itself but meaningless to anyone else, like a novelty search that discovers a thousand variations on the same trick.

But I think there are a few reasons it stays anchored. The first is that these agents don't operate in a vacuum. They're built on top of models trained on the accumulated scientific literature, and that literature is already a distillation of what humans found worth asking. When the agent proposes a hypothesis, it's drawing on the questions, the benchmarks, the open problems that the community has written down. The prior is a human prior.

The second is the feedback loop. The AI Scientist doesn't just generate ideas, it writes them up, and the writeups go through review. Right now that's partly automated and partly human, but either way the evaluation signal is shaped by what reviewers care about: is this novel, is it rigorous, does it matter. If the system is being selected on those criteria, it's hard for it to wander too far from problems people consider relevant.

And the third, which I think is actually the most important, is that we get to design the environment. Open-endedness is not the same as unconstrained. The way I see it, the researcher's role shifts from executing experiments to curating the space of problems and the measures of progress. You decide which domains to point the system at, which datasets, which metrics. That curation is where human values enter, and it's a much higher-leverage place to spend your time than tuning hyperparameters.

So I'm not worried that open-ended agents will drift off into irrelevance. If anything, the harder problem is the opposite: making sure they're open-ended enough that they surprise us, rather than just automating the obvious next step everyone already saw coming.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think that connection is guaranteed by open-endedness itself. You can have a system that keeps generating novel problems and solutions, but those might become increasingly irrelevant to us. So the important question is: what shapes the space it explores?

For an AI Scientist, humans still provide a lot of that structure. We choose the initial research direction, the data and tools it has access to, and the criteria we use to decide whether a result is interesting. Even if the agent autonomously proposes experiments, there’s a connection back to what we want to understand or improve.

And I think that connection needs to be ongoing. You want room for unexpected discoveries, because otherwise you’re just optimizing a very narrow objective. But you also want people to be able to look at the results and say, ‘This is useful; let’s pursue this,’ or, ‘This is technically novel, but it isn’t helping us.’ So I’d see it as a feedback loop between autonomous exploration and human judgment, rather than assuming that an open-ended process will naturally stay relevant.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think open-endedness, by itself, guarantees that connection. You can have a system that keeps discovering novel things, but those things might be completely irrelevant to us. The connection comes from how we set up the process: what environments we put these agents in, what feedback they receive, and which discoveries we choose to build on.

With an AI scientist, humans can still shape the research agenda without specifying every experiment. We might care about a particular disease or about making computation more efficient, while giving the agent freedom to explore approaches we wouldn’t have thought of. So there’s room for open-ended exploration within a direction that matters to people.

But I’d frame that as an ongoing design challenge, rather than something we should assume will happen automatically. You want enough freedom for surprising discoveries, and enough interaction with humans that novelty doesn’t become an end in itself.
